sentences.text: This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights; through it, each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same (for a typical patient from about 20% at 0 to about 88% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher), and a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises the risk to about 42%.

Higher cholesterol (about 12% at 193 mg/dL to about 38% at 308 mg/dL), more ST depression on exercise (about 15% at 0 mm to about 38% at 2.8 mm) and older age (about 17% at 42 to about 22% at 66 years) raise it steadily, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 37%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG to about 35%.

Compared with no chest pain symptoms, typical angina lowers it to about 2%, non-anginal chest pain to about 3% and atypical angina to about 9%; being a woman lowers it to about 1%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 9%, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 29% at 118 to about 15% at 175 beats per minute.

Some rarer results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 2 to 17): a downsloping ST segment raises the risk to about 29%, while a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 14% and an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG to about 16%.

This part combines the angina gate with chest pain type, the ST segment slope and the thallium result, not as a simple sum, and acts on 71 of 242 training patients, all with a flat ST segment (for its typical patient from about 23% without it to about 56% with it).
Through it, chest pain symptoms of any type rather than none raise that patient's risk from about 23% to about 56%, and chest pain on exercise raises it further, from about 56% to about 70%.

Through the angina gate inside it, being a woman or having typical angina raises the risk of the 29 patients the gate acts on, all with chest pain on exercise and a flat ST segment, from about 81% to above 99% for its typical patient.
A thallium result coded 4 raises a typical patient's risk to about 88% with a flat ST segment, against about 31% otherwise (the model has little data on this, n = 2).
One small part, for chest pain on exercise with ST depression, barely changes the predictions.

parts.name: flat_slope_amplifier
parts.original_hypothesis: Two serial ReLUs turn flat ST slope and the angina gate g=665 into a large risk term. In indicator units 3598 = relu(-2.298 + 3.098[flat slope] + 1.288 g) and 1650 = relu(-0.359 - 1.286[asymptomatic cp:4] + 1.944[thal=4] + 1.683*3598). So with flat slope, 1650 = relu(0.988 + 2.168 g) if chest pain is not asymptomatic and relu(-0.298 + 2.168 g) if it is: a flat-slope bonus of 0.99 (logit +1.42) that is withheld for asymptomatic patients (who already get +2.06 from the linear term), plus a slope-gated amplification of the gate (logit +3.1 per unit g). Without flat slope 3598 needs g > 1.78, so 1650 is almost always 0. The thal=4 flag 2011 passes through to the output. EVIDENCE (train, n=242, full sample): 1650 by (flat slope, asymptomatic cp:4, gate fires): (1,0,0) n=42 constant 0.990 (38% positive); (1,1,0) n=40 always 0 (80% positive, already high from linear cp:4 +2.06); (1,0,1) n=4 mean 2.57 (4/4 positive); (1,1,1) n=24 mean 2.71, max 7.59 (83% positive); no flat slope: 0 on 131/132 rows. Removing 1650 entirely: train AUC 0.953 -> 0.919, acc 0.893 -> 0.831; mean logit contribution on gate rows +2.84.
